strapline: Two bail rulings in five days for Mundubile and Zulu; LAZ promises to defend the two-term limit; the UNDP warns on budget taxes; the Chipolopolo in Bujumbura at 15:00

stories.title: Friday for jurisdiction, Tuesday for liberty: the High Court rules on 20 November whether it can hear Mundubile and Zulu's sedition bail plea, and on 24 November on bail for the 18
stories.excerpt: The Lusaka High Court heard the State's objection to the sedition bail application on Monday 16 November and reserved its ruling to Friday 20 November at 09:30. The Director of Public Prosecutions argued that filing in Lusaka while the case sat in Solwezi was an abuse of process; the defence relied on Section 123 of the Criminal Procedure Code. News Diggers reports that the separate constitutional bail application by all 18 treason accused will be decided on Tuesday 24 November, the day Mundubile and Zulu are also due to take plea before a magistrate.

image.label: Two dates, two courts
image.caption: The Lusaka High Court has set 20 November for the jurisdiction question in the sedition bail plea and 24 November for the constitutional bail ruling in the treason matter.

body: Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu, who have been in custody since late August, now have two dates in the coming week on which judges will decide whether and how their applications for release can proceed. The first is Friday 20 November, when the Lusaka High Court rules on a preliminary objection by the State to their bail application in the seditious practices case. The second, reported by News Diggers on Tuesday 17 November, is Tuesday 24 November, when the same court is due to rule on the constitutional bail application brought by Mundubile, Zulu and 16 others held on treason-related allegations at Mukobeko Maximum Correctional Facility. That is also the day the two men are due to take plea on the sedition charges before Lusaka Resident Magistrate Webster Milumbe.

The hearing on Monday 16 November dealt only with the sedition matter. According to the Zambia Monitor, the State, led by Director of Public Prosecutions Gilbert Phiri, asked the court to throw out the bail application. ZNBC's report of the hearing, carried by the Zambian Observer, said the matter was before a three-judge panel led by Judge Mulenga and listed three questions the State wanted answered: whether the Lusaka High Court has jurisdiction when the case was previously before the Solwezi High Court; whether filing a bail application in Lusaka while the case was still in Solwezi amounted to a multiplicity of proceedings; and whether accused persons whose trial is before a Subordinate Court may seek bail from the High Court without first asking the trial court.

The Zambia Monitor reported the State's position as being that the High Court's bail powers do not allow parties to bypass the established procedures for moving cases between courts, and that the Lusaka filing, made while the case was still in Solwezi, **"amounted to a multiplicity of proceedings and an abuse of court process"**. The State also argued that once the case had been transferred to the Lusaka Subordinate Court, any bail request should go there first.

The defence, whose lawyers the Monitor did not name, answered that Section 123 of the Criminal Procedure Code gives the Lusaka High Court jurisdiction to hear the application. They said the Solwezi Subordinate Court had declined jurisdiction, that the referral to the Solwezi High Court concerned only the transfer of the case, and that no bail application had been filed in either Solwezi court, so there was no duplication. The court reserved its ruling to Friday at 09:30 and adjourned the bail application itself until that ruling is given.

The two men face two counts of seditious practices under Section 57 of the Penal Code, arising from Facebook livestreams on 14 August 2026, the day after the general election. The Monitor and the Times of Zambia summarise the counts the same way: Mundubile is alleged to have called on the Electoral Commission of Zambia to announce the winner on the basis of the party's parallel vote tabulation, and Zulu is alleged to have announced that Mundubile would address the nation at a set time. Both are lawyers; neither has yet entered a plea.

The case began in Solwezi, where the defence argued that the alleged offences were committed in Lusaka and that both men were arrested and live there. Principal Resident Magistrate Mambwe Mukonde referred the jurisdiction question to the High Court, and on 5 November Solwezi High Court Judge Edward Musona ordered the matter transferred to Lusaka. When it was called before Magistrate Milumbe on 11 November, the Times of Zambia reported, State Counsel Bonaventure Mutale, Chifumu Banda and Sakwiba Sikota asked to leave the courtroom because they had no instructions from their clients, and the magistrate adjourned plea to 24 November **"in the interest of justice"**.

body.text: The treason matter and the political argument around it

body: The constitutional bail application is a separate proceeding in which all 18 people held over the alleged plot seek release pending trial. News Diggers reports that the ruling is set for 24 November and quotes Sakwiba Sikota describing the security arrangements around the case as **"over-dramatised"**, contrasting it with the Captain Solo treason case, which he said involved more than 70 serving commandos, whereas this one involves three former commandos.

The approach of the rulings has also drawn political comment. Wynter Kabimba, the Economic Front president and a former justice minister, said on Prime Television's Matters Arising programme, in remarks reported by the Zambian Observer and News Diggers on Monday 16 November, that the governing UPND would suffer a backlash if the treason case ended in a nolle prosequi or without any conviction. He said the public expected at least some of the accused to be convicted, and asked how it could otherwise be persuaded of the seriousness of allegations over which the suspects had been held for so long. Neither report carried a response from the UPND or the government.

body.title: The dates
items: Friday 20 November, 09:30 — High Court ruling on the State's objection to the sedition bail application
Tuesday 24 November — High Court ruling on constitutional bail for the 18 treason accused (News Diggers)
Tuesday 24 November — Mundubile and Zulu due to take plea on the sedition charges before Magistrate Milumbe

body.confirmed: The State's preliminary objection to the sedition bail application was heard on Monday 16 November and the ruling is reserved to Friday 20 November at 09:30 (Zambia Monitor; ZNBC via the Zambian Observer). The charges and the Solwezi-to-Lusaka transfer are as reported by the Zambia Monitor and the Times of Zambia. The 24 November plea date was set on 11 November (Times of Zambia).
body.unverified: The 24 November date for the constitutional bail ruling rests on News Diggers' report of 17 November, which is behind a paywall and gives no further detail of Monday's proceedings in that matter. The names of the judges on the sedition bail panel, beyond the presiding Judge Mulenga, were not reported. All charges are allegations: no plea has been taken and nothing has been tested at trial.

stories.title: The lawyers come in: LAZ says it will litigate if need be to keep the two-term limit, as a youth consortium sets a march on Parliament for 25 November and M'membe cries foul
stories.excerpt: News Diggers reports that Law Association of Zambia president Arnold Kaluba has pledged to defend Article 106's two-term limit, by litigation if necessary, and welcomed the Justice Minister's assurance that the Executive will not interfere with the petitions before Parliament. The same day the Zambian Observer carried the Zambia Youth Organisation Consortium's plan for a march from Northmead to Parliament on 25 November, and Fred M'membe's reply calling it neither spontaneous nor organic.

image.label: Article 106
image.caption: The Law Association of Zambia, a youth consortium and the Socialist Party have each staked out positions on the two-term limit within a day of one another.

body: The Law Association of Zambia has taken a position on presidential term limits, two weeks after its members and the Socialist Party asked it to. News Diggers reported on Tuesday 17 November that LAZ president Arnold Kaluba said the association would defend the two-term limit in Article 106 of the Constitution and would take legal action if necessary to stop any attempt to remove it. Kaluba urged members of Parliament to look beyond immediate political circumstances and to weigh the long-term effects of removing the limit on democracy, accountability and stability. He also welcomed Justice Minister Jack Mwiimbu's statement last week that the Executive will not interfere with Parliament's handling of the petitions seeking its removal. The Diggers report is behind a paywall, and the full text of the statement was not available.

The statement answers two requests made at the start of the month. On 2 November, the Zambia Monitor reported, Socialist Party president Fred M'membe wrote to LAZ asking it to convene an extraordinary general meeting on any amendment to Article 106 and to state its position within seven days. On 3 November, the Zambian Observer reported, three members, Linda Kasonde, the Chapter One Foundation executive director and a former LAZ president, Josiah Kalala and Henry Mulenga, lodged a formal requisition under the association's rules for an extraordinary meeting to adopt resolutions reaffirming a maximum of two five-year terms, opposing any extension and any application of a change to a sitting president, and authorising advocacy and litigation. The requisition recalled LAZ's part in the Oasis Forum that opposed a third term for Frederick Chiluba in 2001.

body.text: A march for removal, and its critics

body: On the other side of the argument, the Zambian Observer on Monday 16 November carried a report, credited to The People's Brief, that the Zambia Youth Organisation Consortium plans a march from Northmead bus station to the Parliament Buildings on Wednesday 25 November in support of removing the limit. The consortium's vice-chairperson, Boas Kanyama, said 63,151 young people from all ten provinces were expected, that the police had been formally notified and that about 500 officers were expected to provide security. The numbers are the consortium's own and no other outlet had reported the plan by Tuesday morning. **"As a consortium, we will not be reduced to a political party,"** Kanyama was quoted as saying, adding that the march was about Zambians exercising a democratic right rather than about a third term.

The consortium is the body that presented a petition to Parliament on 28 October through nominated MP Francis Kope, according to the Zambia Monitor; it had first announced its request for a private member's motion on Article 106(3) in September. M'membe responded to the march announcement in an article published by the Zambian Observer the same evening. He called the plan **"neither spontaneous nor organic"** and a **"calculated, state-sponsored assault on Zambia's constitutional order"**, asked who was funding it, and said young people should not be used as **"cheap foot soldiers"**. He contrasted the police escort on offer with what he said were the difficulties opposition parties and civil society face in obtaining permits, repeated his call for a referendum on any change, and demanded that President Hakainde Hichilema **"state clearly and publicly that he will neither seek nor accept a third term"**.

The government's position has not changed. Mwiimbu has said the petitions are a matter for Parliament and that the Executive will not interfere. State House, through Chief Communications Specialist Clayson Hamasaka, has said that the President neither initiated nor influenced the campaign: **"This has nothing to do with the head of State, so why should he be dragged into it?"** Opposition leader Given Lubinda has called for a national referendum. Wynter Kabimba of the Economic Front, in remarks reported by News Diggers on Monday, said removing the limit would be a bad idea and could split the UPND itself.

What happens next depends on the National Assembly, which has yet to say how or when the petitions will be dealt with, and on LAZ, which has not said what form any litigation would take or at what stage it would be filed.

stories.title: 'Mapanza should not be left behind': Hichilema promises a dam on the Munyeke and Ng'onga rivers for wheat, says Zambia has never been better, and gives a school over K1 million
stories.excerpt: On Sunday 15 November the President closed his Southern Province weekend at St Mark's in Mapanza, Mbabala Constituency. The Times of Zambia reports a promise of strategic dams, boreholes and health facilities; News Diggers reports his warning against social-media lies; a UPND Media Team account carried by the Zambian Observer names the rivers, a wheat ambition and the donations.

image.label: Water for Mapanza
image.caption: The President told residents of Mapanza Chiefdom that a dam would let them grow wheat and keep the country a food producer.

body: President Hakainde Hichilema ended a weekend in Southern Province on Sunday 15 November in Mapanza, in Mbabala Constituency near Choma, where he promised water infrastructure and told residents the country was in better shape than at any time before. The Times of Zambia described the event as a rally on the grounds of St Mark's Secondary School before hundreds of residents and supporters; News Diggers called it a community engagement; a UPND Media Team account published by the Zambian Observer placed his remarks at a service at St Mark's Anglican Church. All three agree on the substance.

The Times reported the President's promise that the government would build strategic dams to support irrigation, production and food security, alongside health facilities and boreholes across the country, with Mbabala among the beneficiaries. **"Mapanza should not be left behind,"** he said, and went on: **"That is why your Government is deliberately constructing strategic dams, just like in other parts of the country, so that we remain a food producer and ensure national food security."** He said the people of Mapanza Chiefdom had **"the potential to grow wheat and other crops, thereby contributing to national food security and the broader agricultural transformation agenda"**, and framed the UPND's win on 13 August as a mandate for development.

body.text: The rivers, the wheat and the gifts

body: The UPND Media Team text carried by the Observer adds the detail the Times does not. It says the dam will be built on the Munyeke and Ng'onga rivers, that the Grow Zambia agenda targets a million tonnes of wheat, and that the President told the gathering he had himself harvested 400 hectares of wheat in the area, urging farmers to use the dam for the crop because **"water will now be available"**. It also records that the President and the First Family gave more than K1 million to St Mark's Secondary School for the rehabilitation of its kitchen and hall, pledged to rehabilitate the school's borehole, and gave K200,000 to the church and K100,000 to its choir. Mbabala MP Joseph Munsanje announced the donations; Chief Mapanza's representative, Godrick Simachenya, and head teacher Mervis Ntalasha also spoke. Because the account comes from the governing party's own media team, the figures are its figures.

News Diggers, in its report on Monday 16 November, concentrated on the political message. Hichilema told the gathering that Zambia had never been better than it is now, urged people not to be cheated, and warned them against listening to those spreading lies on social media, which he said would set the country back. He said development was under way and that the country was now respected abroad. The Observer's text likewise has him accusing the opposition of propaganda and calling for unity behind the Grow Zambia agenda, which he said needed **"concerted efforts from all Zambians"**.

The Mapanza stop came two days after the President's public engagement in Choma on Friday 13 November, at which, the Times reported, he said farmers owed by the Food Reserve Agency would be paid within 10 to 15 days and repeated the promise of strategic dams nationwide. None of Sunday's reports gave a cost, a timetable or a contractor for the Mapanza dam.

stories.title: 'Not solely on how much revenue it generates': the UNDP asks the Treasury to shield poor households from the 2027 budget's taxes, as farmers decry the mobile money levy
stories.excerpt: At the launch of a 2027 Budget Highlights Report in Lusaka on Monday 16 November, UNDP resident representative James Wakiaga urged government to keep VAT zero-rating on basic foods and to cushion low-income households against higher VAT, a doubled mobile money levy and new tariffs. The ZNFU says it received the budget with 'heightened anxiety'; News Diggers has set out the levy bands and a passport fee rising to K1,000.

image.label: The cost of the budget
image.caption: The UNDP wants the 2027 budget judged by its effect on poverty and welfare as well as by the revenue it raises.

body: The United Nations Development Programme has asked the government to think again about the revenue measures in the 2027 budget that fall most heavily on ordinary households. Launching a 2027 Budget Highlights Report in Lusaka on Monday 16 November, UNDP resident representative James Wakiaga said the budget marked a shift from stabilisation to growth, but that its tax measures needed careful implementation so as not to add to the financial pressure on low-income families and small businesses. The Zambia Monitor reported him listing the measures of concern as the increase in value added tax, the higher mobile money levy, new tariffs on selected essential commodities and the reduction of tax relief on energy-saving appliances.

**"Fiscal policy should not be assessed solely on how much revenue it generates,"** Wakiaga said, arguing that it should also be judged by its effect on poverty, inequality and welfare. He asked the Treasury to keep basic foods zero-rated for VAT and to adopt targeted safeguards, including adjustments to social cash transfers, and said growth **"should generate private sector investment, decent jobs for young people"**. He credited Zambia with restoring macroeconomic stability and dealing with unsustainable external debt, and said living standards were the next test. At the same event Chipengo Zulu, director of corporate affairs at Zambian Breweries, said excise duties on plastic bottles, bottle caps and industrial sugar would raise production costs and prices and weaken local manufacturers against imports.

News Diggers set out the mobile money proposal on Sunday 15 November: the levy would double in every band, so that a transaction of up to K150 would attract K0.64 instead of K0.32, and a transfer of between K5,000 and K10,000 would attract K16 instead of K8. The same report says an ordinary 32-page passport would cost K1,000 in 2027 instead of K666.68, with a new two-day premium service at K5,000; the fee was last revised in August 2008 and government attributes the increase to higher production costs. The Mobile Money Association of Zambia had already objected on 7 November, its president Chris Sichende telling the Zambia Monitor the higher levy could **"erode the gains made so far in terms of financial inclusion expansion"** and asking for wider consultation.

The farmers' union has made the same point. Harad Lungu, executive director of the Zambia National Farmers' Union, told the 2027 National Budget Symposium last week that **"the Union has received the proposed 2027 national budget with caution and heightened anxiety"**, and said the levy increase would hurt farmers and discourage the use of digital financial services, News Diggers reported. The Civil Society for Poverty Reduction, in the same report, opposed turning the Farmer Input Support Programme into a loan scheme.

The debate comes with the currency under mild pressure. The Zambia Monitor reported on Monday that the kwacha closed the week to Friday 13 November just below K20.50 to the US dollar, a weekly loss of 0.67 per cent and the largest since the week ending 16 October, as demand for foreign exchange outweighed supply and the dollar held near its strongest level since May 2025 on expectations of tighter United States monetary policy. Neither report carried a government response to the UNDP's recommendations, and the levy and fee changes remain proposals for 2027 rather than measures in force.

stories.title: A 54 per cent maize collapse and 23-hour blackouts, written into the books: the IMF credits Zambia with budgeting for climate risk and sets an October 2027 deadline
stories.excerpt: An IMF technical assistance report on climate change and fiscal risks, dated October 2026 and publicised by the Treasury on Monday 16 November, says Zambia has made notable progress in writing climate shocks into public financial management. It records that the 2023–24 drought cut maize output by 54 per cent and pushed load-shedding to 23 hours a day, and asks for a quantified climate fiscal risk assessment by October 2027 and coverage of floods and storms by October 2028.

image.label: Drought in the ledger
image.caption: The IMF report puts drought-related spending at about 1 per cent of GDP in 2024 and 0.3 per cent in 2025.

body: The International Monetary Fund has given Zambia credit for the way it now accounts for drought, and set it two deadlines. Its technical assistance report, 'Zambia – Climate Change and Fiscal Risks', dated October 2026 and publicised by the Ministry of Finance and National Planning on Monday 16 November, says the country has made notable progress in integrating climate risks into public financial management, with better transparency, coordination between institutions and capacity to assess what climate shocks do to the economy. The Zambia Monitor and the Zambian Observer both reported the document and the minister's statement on Monday evening.

The report's starting point is the 2023–24 drought. It records that maize production fell by 54 per cent and that load-shedding reached 23 hours a day, and it puts drought-related spending at about 1 per cent of GDP in 2024 and 0.3 per cent in 2025. With hydropower making up about 80 per cent of installed generating capacity, it says, agriculture and mining remain exposed to prolonged dry spells, though it acknowledges the government's efforts to add solar and wind capacity.

body.text: What has been built, and what is asked

body: The IMF singles out the Fiscal Risk Statement, first published with the 2025 budget, as a major step in transparency, and notes that the 2026 statement added a climate fiscal risk register covering agriculture, electricity generation, mining, infrastructure and public revenue and spending. During a mission to Lusaka from 24 June to 3 July 2026, Fund staff worked with Zambian officials on a tool known as Q-CRAFT, the Quantitative Climate Risk Assessment Fiscal Tool, which models how climate scenarios would affect growth, revenue, expenditure and public debt.

The recommendations are dated. Zambia should publish its first quantified climate-related fiscal risk assessment by October 2027, and by October 2028 should strengthen its drought analysis and extend the assessment to floods and storms. The report also asks for a better risk register, clearer institutional responsibilities, stronger coordination between agencies and the alignment of adaptation investment with long-term financing.

Finance and National Planning Minister Situmbeko Musokotwane tied the report to the 2027 budget. **"Our transition from economic stabilisation to sustained growth demands stronger protection against climate shocks,"** he said in a statement on Monday, adding that **"climate resilience is therefore integral to fiscal resilience and central to the 2027 National Budget theme"**, which is 'Grow Zambia: From Stabilisation to Unlocking Opportunities, Creating Jobs and Improving Livelihoods for All'. Neither report quoted IMF staff directly, and the report is a technical assistance document rather than a programme review.

stories.title: Ten held and four wanted over a hijacked copper truck: police say the Kafulafuta load was offloaded at a Twapia yard and the driver was promised US$200,000
stories.excerpt: Police spokesperson Chipo Kaitisha said on Monday 16 November that ten people, including the truck driver and four employees of an Ndola bonded warehouse, had been arrested over a truckload of copper blisters reported hijacked in Kafulafuta on 9 November, and that four more suspects, two of them foreign nationals, were being sought. The quantity and value of the copper have not been given.

image.label: The Kafulafuta load
image.caption: Police say a hijacked copper consignment was offloaded in Twapia and moved on in two tipper trucks.

body: Police have arrested ten people over the alleged hijacking of a truck carrying copper blisters and are looking for four more. In a statement issued in Lusaka on Monday 16 November, reported by News Diggers and the Zambia Monitor, Police Public Relations Officer Chipo Kaitisha said the incident was reported on 9 November in Kafulafuta District, and that the truck and its trailers were later found abandoned near the Kafulafuta police checkpoint without their load.

According to the Monitor's account of the statement, preliminary investigations indicate that the copper was offloaded at a haulage yard in Twapia, Ndola, and moved on in two tipper trucks. The ten arrested include the driver of the truck and four employees of a bonded warehouse in Ndola. Police allege that the driver had been promised US$200,000 for his part. The four still being sought are described as a Tanzanian national alleged to be behind the theft, a Congolese national alleged to have recruited the driver, the alleged owner of the Twapia yard and the reported owner of one of the tipper trucks. Lusaka Brief does not name them: none has been charged before a court.

Kaitisha appealed to the public, and in particular to residents of Kafulafuta, Ndola and Kitwe, for information about the four and about the whereabouts of the copper, saying anyone with information should **"report to the nearest police station"** and that it would be treated in confidence. She said the suspects would be brought before the courts.

The statement leaves a good deal unsaid. Neither report gives the tonnage or value of the consignment, the name of the company that owned the copper or the truck, where the load was bound, how the hijacking was carried out, whether any copper has been recovered, or the specific charges the ten arrested will face. News Diggers' report is behind a paywall and the visible text ends in the middle of the police statement. Blister copper is an intermediate smelter product, which is why the consignment's weight and grade matter to any estimate of what was taken.

body.confirmed: Ten arrests, a manhunt for four and the 9 November Kafulafuta report are in the police statement as carried by News Diggers and the Zambia Monitor. The Twapia offloading, the tipper trucks and the US$200,000 promise are what the police say their preliminary investigations indicate.
body.unverified: The quantity, value and ownership of the copper; the charges; whether any of the metal has been recovered. The roles attributed to the four wanted people are police allegations and none has been charged.

stories.title: A TikTok video from September, a charge under the Cyber Crimes Act in November: Ndola police arrest a 35-year-old woman over remarks about the President and release her on bond
stories.excerpt: Police in Ndola say a 35-year-old woman from Twapia has been charged with using a computer system to commit an offence, under Section 20 of the Cyber Crimes Act No. 4 of 2025 read with Section 179 of the Penal Code, over a TikTok video posted on 9 September that they say contained insulting remarks about President Hichilema. She is on police bond and is yet to appear in court; Lusaka Brief is not naming her.

image.label: Section 20
image.caption: The Cyber Crimes Act of 2025 is the law under which Ndola police have charged a woman over a TikTok video about the President.

body: A 35-year-old woman from Twapia township in Ndola has been arrested and charged over a TikTok video that police say insulted President Hakainde Hichilema. The arrest was announced by Police Public Relations Officer Chipo Kaitisha in a statement on Monday 16 November and reported by News Diggers and the Zambian Observer. Lusaka Brief does not name her: she has not yet appeared before a court.

The charge is the use of a computer or computer system to commit an offence, contrary to Section 20 of the Cyber Crimes Act No. 4 of 2025, read with Section 179 of the Penal Code. According to the police statement as carried by the Observer, the video was posted on 9 September 2026 between 18:00 and 22:00 from a TikTok account, and police allege that she acted jointly with other persons unknown. The statement said the video **"contained insulting remarks directed at the Republican President, Mr Hakainde Hichilema"**, and that she had been **"released on police bond and is expected to appear in court soon"**.

No court date has been given, and nothing has been reported from the woman herself, her family or any lawyer. News Diggers' report is behind a paywall and the visible text ends before the facts of the case; the Observer carried the police statement in full. Neither report says what the video contained beyond the police description, or why the arrest came more than two months after the posting.

The next step is a first appearance before a magistrate in Ndola, where the charge would be read and a plea taken, and where any application to vary the bond or to challenge the charge would be made. Until then the public record consists of a single police statement: an allegation, the section of the law relied on, the date of the posting and the fact of release on bond. The woman is presumed innocent, and the question of what was said in the video, and whether it amounts to an offence under Section 20, is one for the court. Lusaka Brief will name her only if and when she is charged before a court and named by at least two established outlets.

body.confirmed: The arrest, the age and township of the accused, the charge and the police bond are in the police statement as carried by News Diggers and the Zambian Observer.
body.unverified: The content of the video beyond the police description; the identity of the 'other persons unknown'; the court date; the accused's response. The charge is an allegation.

stories.title: 'Burundi managed to play when we had huge support, so why can't we play?': Zambia face Burundi at Stade Intwari at 15:00 today with second place in Group I to protect
stories.excerpt: Four days after the 1–1 draw in Ndola, the Chipolopolo meet Burundi again in Bujumbura this afternoon. Interim coach George Lwandamina says preparations are complete and the young side is 'in a building process'; defender Mathews Banda says a hostile crowd will not intimidate them. Zambia have four points to Algeria's seven, with Togo on three and Burundi on two.

image.label: Bujumbura, 15:00
image.caption: Zambia play the return leg against Burundi at Stade Intwari with second place in Group I at stake.

body: The Chipolopolo play Burundi at Stade Intwari in Bujumbura at 15:00 Central Africa Time today, Tuesday 17 November, in the return fixture of their 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifying double-header. Friday's first meeting at home ended 1–1, and the standings reported by FAZ Media and ZamFoot leave Algeria on seven points, Zambia on four, Togo on three and Burundi on two in Group I. The top two in each group go to the finals in Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda.

Interim coach George Lwandamina told FAZ Media on the eve of the game that the technical bench had done its work. **"We have already done our part; we have prepared so well and are raring to go for the game,"** he said, in remarks published by ZamFoot on Tuesday morning. He described the squad as young and still learning one another: **"We are in a building process. This team is very young and the players have begun to understand each other,"** adding that **"the chemistry in every team which is starting cannot be 100%."** He said the players' attitude and character had carried them since the points dropped in Algeria.

Mathews Banda, the Czech Republic-based defender, spoke to FAZ Media after Monday's training session and was unbothered by the prospect of a hostile ground. **"Burundi managed to play when we had huge support, so why can't we play?"** he said. He reported that the squad had recovered well and that **"the concentration is just on Tuesday's game"**, and reflected on Friday's draw: **"On Friday, we just played well but things just did not work out."** Asked what the team needed, he said simply that **"we just need a win, but we are mindful of the different possibilities in football"**, and appealed to supporters not to give up on the side.

Neither FAZ Media piece carried team news, injuries or a confirmed line-up, and Lwandamina gave no hint of his starting eleven. The arithmetic is simple enough. A win takes Zambia to seven points; a draw leaves them on five, still second for now; a defeat lifts Burundi to five points and above Zambia, and would leave the Chipolopolo looking over their shoulder at Togo as well. The result will be in Wednesday's edition.

stories.title: Twenty-three tracks and half the industry: Rich Bizzy's 'Africa' gathers Chef 187, Macky 2, Chile One and JK, while Prince Luv and Yo Maps release 'Over'
stories.excerpt: Two of the week's Zambian releases lean on collaboration. The Zambia Monitor reports that Rich Bizzy's new album 'Africa' runs to 23 tracks across Afrobeat, Kalindula, Amapiano and R&B with a long list of guests, and that Prince Luv and Yo Maps have followed 'Show Me Love' and 'Imbwa Ndine' with an Afro-pop single about letting a relationship go.

image.label: New releases
image.caption: Rich Bizzy's 23-track 'Africa' and the Prince Luv–Yo Maps single 'Over' lead the week's Zambian releases.

body: Rich Bizzy has released an album built on the idea that Zambian music is now a team sport. 'Africa', which the Zambia Monitor reported on Sunday 15 November as having come out the previous week, runs to 23 tracks and ranges across Afrobeat, Kalindula, Amapiano and R&B. The guest list reads like a roll-call of the country's charts: Chef 187, Chile One Mr Zambia, Triple M, JK, Bobby East, Towela, Macky 2, T-Sean, Chester, Blood Kid and Afunika are all named, among others.

The Monitor picks out several pairings. 'Mailo' features Chile One Mr Zambia; 'I Lose My Mind' has Triple M; 'Wako Ni Wako' brings in Chef 187; 'Wele' puts JK and Bobby East on the same track; and 'Biggie Bokosi' features Blood Kid. Among the solo cuts are 'Yaweh', 'Gen Z', 'Baletumwenamo' and 'Let Me Enjoy'. The paper describes the record's themes as resilience, unity and African identity, and treats it as a further sign of how much of the local industry's output now rests on collaboration. No label was named and the full track list was not published.

body.text: Prince Luv and Yo Maps, again

body: The other release the Monitor reported on Sunday is 'Over', a three-minute-35-second Afro-pop single by Prince Luv with Yo Maps, released on Friday, the Monitor reported on Sunday 15 November. Produced by Kingtec under Prince Luv Entertainment and Africori, it is a song about a relationship that has ended and the case for accepting it and moving on: Prince Luv carries the heartbreak in the verses and Yo Maps supplies a chorus about closure. It extends a partnership that has already produced 'Show Me Love', 'On The Low' and 'Imbwa Ndine'.

Neither artist was quoted in the Monitor's reports, and no sales or streaming figures were given for either release. What the two have in common is the method: an established artist spreading 23 tracks across a dozen guests, and two established names returning to a pairing that has worked for them before. On the Monitor's reading, that is where Zambian popular music now is, with collaboration the rule rather than the exception.

analysis.title: Friday's ruling is about doors, not liberty
analysis.body: It is worth being precise about what the High Court decides on 20 November. The question is not whether Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu should be released on the sedition charges; it is whether the Lusaka High Court is the right door to knock on at all. The State's case has a tidy logic: the file now sits with a Lusaka magistrate, the normal route is to ask the trial court first, and a High Court application lodged while the case was still in Solwezi looks like two bites at one cherry. The defence has an equally tidy reply: Section 123 of the Criminal Procedure Code gives the High Court power to grant bail, the Solwezi courts never heard a bail application, so there is nothing to duplicate. If the objection succeeds, the application goes to Magistrate Milumbe and the clock starts again. If it fails, the court moves to the merits of release pending trial. The 24 November constitutional bail ruling for all 18 is the larger event, because it goes to the length of detention itself. Watch, too, whether plea is finally taken that day, or whether a further adjournment follows.

analysis.title: What LAZ can and cannot do about Article 106
analysis.body: The Law Association's promise of litigation changes the register of the term-limit argument from rallies to pleadings, but its reach should not be overstated. Parliament may amend Article 106 by the two-thirds route in Article 79; no court can stop MPs voting. What LAZ can do is test the process in court: above all whether the public consultation the Constitutional Court stressed in its June 2025 judgment on Bill 7 has taken place, and whether a change could lawfully benefit a sitting president. Supporters of removal have a case to make too. Boas Kanyama's consortium says the ballot, not a clause, should decide who governs, and that a petition to Parliament is the constitutional way to ask. The government says it is standing aside, and the Justice Minister's assurance of non-interference is now being quoted approvingly by LAZ itself. The critics' case rests on 2001, on four constitutional review bodies that kept two terms, and on the question Fred M'membe keeps asking: who is paying for 63,151 marchers and 500 police officers. What to watch is procedural: whether the Assembly tables the petitions, whether any MP sponsors a bill, and whether LAZ holds the extraordinary meeting its members have requisitioned.

analysis.title: The UNDP's test for the 2027 budget
analysis.body: James Wakiaga's intervention is polite and pointed. The UNDP is not disputing that the Treasury needs revenue; it is asking that each measure be weighed by who pays. On the government's side the case is real: the budget's stated aim is to broaden the tax base and raise domestic revenue, an El Niño season has to be financed, and the stability the UNDP itself credits was bought with discipline. Broad, low-rate levies on mobile money and VAT are efficient precisely because almost everyone pays them. On the other side, the Mobile Money Association, the farmers' union and now the UNDP make the same point from different angles: a levy that doubles on a K150 transfer falls hardest on the people drawn into formal finance by its cheapness, and a passport at K1,000 is a 50 per cent increase on a document many need for work. The UNDP's suggested compromise, keep basic foods zero-rated and raise social cash transfers to match, can still be made before the measures take effect in 2027. The kwacha's drift towards K20.50 adds imported-price pressure on the same households. Watch whether the Treasury answers the UNDP, and what the farmers and the operators do next.
